theme: Incomplete conquest; the cycle begins; the first judges
readingInstruction: Read Judges 1:1-3:31. This is the longest reading of the week, and it introduces a new era. Notice how the book begins by mirroring Joshua, then slowly shows decline. Pay special attention to 2:6-3:6, which gives the key to the whole book, and to the stories of Othniel, Ehud, and Shamgar.
settingTheScene: Joshua is dead, and a whole generation passes. The book of Judges tells what happens next. It covers roughly three hundred years, from the death of Joshua to just before the monarchy, and it is a dark and honest account. Israel has the land but not the faithfulness to keep it. The opening chapter reports tribe-by-tribe incomplete conquest. The next chapters explain why: Israel’s failure to drive out the nations and its habit of worshiping their gods. The book then introduces a repeating pattern that will shape every story to come. This is the most important thing to grasp as you start Judges. The stories are not about heroes. They are about a people who keep forgetting, and a God who keeps saving.
observation: After Joshua’s death, Israel asks the LORD, “Who shall go up first for us against the Canaanites?” and the LORD says Judah (1:1-2).
The first chapter lists repeated failures: “did not drive out” appears again and again (1:19, 21, 27-33).
The angel of the LORD at Bochim rebukes Israel for making covenants with the inhabitants and not breaking down their altars (2:1-5).
“There arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel” (2:10).
Israel “did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals” (2:11).
The pattern: sin, oppression, cry for help, deliverance by a judge, rest, then relapse (2:11-19).
Othniel, Caleb’s nephew, delivers Israel and the land has rest forty years (3:7-11).
Ehud, a left-handed Benjaminite, kills the fat king Eglon (3:12-30). Shamgar strikes down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad (3:31).
interpretation:
The book of Judges opens with an echo and a shadow. The question, “Who shall go up first for us?” mirrors the opening of Joshua, and God’s answer is Judah, just as Genesis 49 would suggest. For a few verses, it seems the conquest will continue. But the language quickly changes. “Did not drive out.” This phrase becomes the drumbeat of the chapter, a quiet record of compromise. The tribes of Benjamin, Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan each fail to dislodge the Canaanites. The theme is partial obedience. Israel is not rebelling openly, but it is settling for less than God had commanded.

The angel of the LORD arrives at Bochim, “the weepers,” and gives the reason. Israel had made treaties with the people of the land and left their altars standing. They were warned. The consequences are described: the nations will become thorns and their gods a snare. The people weep, and offer a sacrifice, but there is no real repentance. This will be a pattern.

The center of the section is 2:6-3:6, which is the theological preface to the whole book. The generation of Joshua dies, and another arises that “did not know the LORD or the work that he had done.” This is one of the saddest sentences in the Bible. The faith was not handed down. Joshua had built the memorial stones, but the story was not told. Then the cycle begins. Israel does evil, God gives them into the hands of oppressors, they cry out, and God raises up a judge to save them. But when the judge dies, the people go back, and they do so even worse than their fathers. The pattern is a spiral downward.

It is important to see that the judges are not moral exemplars. They are “saviors” whom God raises up, flawed and often surprising. Othniel is the one clean example, a faithful man from Caleb’s family. Ehud is a trickster who uses his left hand and a hidden blade. Shamgar is a rough farmer with an oxgoad. The point is not their virtue but God’s compassion. Judges 2:18 says, “the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning.” God saves not because Israel deserves it but because he is merciful.

Why does God leave some nations in the land? Judges 2:22 and 3:1-4 say it was to test Israel, to see whether they would keep the way of the LORD, and to teach war to the generations who had not known it. The testing exposes the heart. And it creates a longing. If these saviors are so flawed and the people so fickle, we begin to ask for a better savior and a king who will truly lead. Judges is the book that makes the reader long for Christ.
connection: The failure to drive out the nations contradicts Deuteronomy 7:1-6 and Joshua 23:12-13. The loss of memory in 2:10 contrasts with Deuteronomy 6:4-9, 20-25. The cycle pattern echoes Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. Othniel’s story ties back to Joshua 15:16-19. The repeated “cry out” and God’s pity recall Exodus 2:23-25. The judges anticipate the greater Savior of Luke 1:68-75.
application:
First, consider the failure to pass on the faith. If you have children, grandchildren, or others you are discipling, ask what you are doing to tell them what God has done. Plan one concrete step this week, such as sharing a testimony or reading a psalm together.

Second, examine your own cycle. We all have patterns: sin, consequences, a cry for help, forgiveness, and, too often, a return. Where do you see this? Ask the Lord to help you move from regret to repentance and from repentance to a changed life.

Third, take comfort in God’s pity. He was “moved to pity by their groaning.” He still is. Bring your groaning to him without hiding it.
prayerPrompts: Confess partial obedience and a short memory, as you see them in your own heart.
Ask him to teach you to tell the next generation what he has done.
Thank him that he is moved to pity by his people’s groaning.
